svg.title: STRIDE applied to network infrastructure, with a concrete example and the control that answers each letter
svg.desc: Six rows. Spoofing: an attacker forges OSPF hellos or an ARP reply and claims an identity - answered by authentication, DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection. Tampering: an unauthenticated BGP update or a modified configuration file changes data in transit - answered by protocol authentication, rollback, integrity checks. Repudiation: nobody can prove who changed the ACL at 02:00 - answered by TACACS+ command accounting and accurate time. Information disclosure: a mirrored port or an unencrypted management protocol exposes credentials - answered by encryption, management plane separation, no cleartext SNMP. Denial of service: a control plane flood or a broadcast storm stops forwarding - answered by CoPP, storm control, rate limits. Elevation of privilege: a low-privilege login reaches enable, or a guest VLAN reaches the core - answered by role permissions, privilege levels, segmentation. Bottom: the five attack surfaces to enumerate - identity, network path, device management, supply chain, and the human process. A footer notes that a STRIDE table without a device name in every row is a poster, not a threat model.
svg.text: STRIDE is only useful when every row names a device and a control
The generic table is a poster. The version below is the one that produces a configuration.
WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE ON NETWORK GEAR
forged OSPF hellos, a gratuitous ARP claiming the gateway,
a DHCP server that is not yours
unauthenticated BGP updates, a config file edited on the
TFTP server, a firmware image with no checksum
nobody can prove who deleted the ACL at 02:00, or the log
a mirrored port left enabled, SNMPv1 community "public",
telnet to the core, a config backup on a share
a control plane flood, a broadcast storm, a BPDU flood,
an ARP scan that exhausts the table
a read-only login that reaches enable, a guest VLAN with a
route to the core, an unprotected console port
Each threat row should end with a device name and a test case, otherwise the model stays on the wall and never reaches a configuration file.
